1.pericope_label: O God, my heart is fixed; I will sing and give praise, even with my glory... For thy mercy is great above the heavens: and thy truth reacheth unto the clouds

schools.summary: Delitzsch alone asks who did the compiling, holding that the psalm is inscribed to David only because assembled from Davidic materials, that the missing direction to the choirmaster suggests a later hand, and that the two pieces are placed side by side rather than soldered together; he rejects outright the proposal that David compiled a third song from two of his own.

Gill supplies little beyond cross-references to the source psalms, but records the one textual difference in the fourth verse, where the source reads unto the heavens and this reads above them; Calvin declines exposition altogether as superfluous, having already written on the two originals.

Clarke gives the verse numbers on both sides of the join and refers the reader back to his earlier notes, judges the variations of little moment, and proposes that the captives in Babylon assembled the psalm and applied it to their own hoped-for restoration.

Henry proceeds as though nothing were borrowed and expounds the opening verses straight through, in successive heads on the manner of praise — fixedness, freeness, fervency, publicness — and on the mercy and truth of the fourth verse; Spurgeon locates the real difference from the source not in the wording but in the position of the verses, praise here preceding prayer instead of growing out of it.
Augustine states the compilation, declines a fresh exposition, marks the seam between the two borrowed halves, and then works the small verbal variations between this psalm and its sources.

debates.question: Who assembled the psalm out of the two earlier ones?

positions.view: Not David; a poet compiling a third song out of two of his own is not conceivable, and the missing choirmaster's heading suggests a later hand.
Probably the captives in Babylon, applying it to their own case, though the Hebrew and all the versions give it to David.
The question is not raised; the psalm is expounded as it stands.

debates.question: Does a compiled psalm need its own exposition?

positions.view: No; having expounded the two sources, it would be superfluous to repeat the work.
Yes, because the same words in a new position carry a different force, praise here preceding prayer rather than following it.
The psalm is simply expounded on its own terms, the borrowing going unmentioned.
The variations themselves repay attention, even where the substance is repeated.

outliers.note: Observes that the one important alteration in the opening verses is a change of divine name detectable in English only by the capitals, and builds his whole reading on the changed position of the verses rather than their wording.
Names and rejects a scholar's proposal that David himself made this psalm out of two of his own, calling the idea not conceivable.

themes: O God, my heart is fixed; I will sing and give praise, even with my glory.
Awake, psaltery and harp: I myself will awake early.
I will praise thee, O Lord, among the people: and I will sing praises unto thee among the nations.
For thy mercy is great above the heavens: and thy truth reacheth unto the clouds.

6.pericope_label: That thy beloved may be delivered: save with thy right hand, and answer me... God hath spoken in his holiness; I will rejoice, I will divide Shechem, and mete out the valley of Succoth

schools.summary: Gill contributes only the seam, noting in a line that from this verse to the end the words are drawn out of the earlier psalm and sending the reader to his notes there.

Clarke passes over the verses themselves and stops at one Hebrew phrase, recording the construction by which speaking in holiness becomes speaking in his Holy One, and referring it to the prophet who foretold the captivity and its term.

Henry reads the whole second half as a school of prayer — public-spirited, resting on the divine power and the divine promise, and content to be answered in the church's deliverance rather than its own; Spurgeon dwells on the relation of the petition to the praise before it and on the weight borne by a man who prays in a representative position.

debates.question: What is meant by God speaking in his holiness?

positions.view: In his holy word, to which he has sworn by his holiness, so that performance is as certain as the promise.
Some read the Hebrew as in his Holy One, referring the words to the prophet who predicted the captivity, its seventy years, and the deliverance.

debates.question: How does this prayer stand to the praise that precedes it?

positions.view: Prayer follows praise and draws strength of faith and holy boldness from it; it is frequently best to begin worship with a hymn.
The relation goes unremarked; the second half is simply taken as instruction in how to pray.
Only the fact of the borrowing is registered, with the exposition left to the source psalm.

outliers.note: Presses the singular pronouns of the petition into an account of representative prayer, where a whole nation may hang upon the petitions of one man, so that pleading for the beloved is easy yet solemn.
Leaves the verse unexpounded and offers instead a construal of one Hebrew word that turns the divine oath into a reference to a named prophet.

themes: That thy beloved may be delivered: save with thy right hand, and answer me.
God hath spoken in his holiness; I will rejoice, I will divide Shechem, and mete out the valley of Succoth.
